claims.text: Phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys is predominantly governed by nanoscale chemical short-range order clusters.
Nanoscale SRO clusters locally reduce lattice distortion.
Nanoscale SRO clusters modify defect interactions.
SRO clusters suppress unwanted phase separation.
SRO clusters promote retention of a stable single-phase microstructure.
SRO-mediated phase stability retains high-temperature strength.
SRO-mediated phase stability retains environmental resistance.
SRO-mediated phase stability retains radiation tolerance.
SRO-mediated phase stability retains cryogenic toughness.
Rapid solidification minimizes SRO formation and produces an approximately random atomic distribution in the proposed baseline.
Annealing at approximately 0.5–0.7 T_m promotes SRO formation.
An intermediate-temperature anneal can form SRO without causing long-range ordering or brittle intermetallic precipitation.
Preferential local bonding between Al and transition metals such as Co or Cr forms the proposed SRO clusters.
SRO clusters act as sinks for point defects.
SRO lowers local free energy by mitigating strain associated with atomic-size mismatch.
SRO provides favorable sites for defect recombination.
Strain mitigation and enhanced defect recombination retard phase decomposition during high-temperature exposure and irradiation.
SRO sustains dislocation mobility and toughening mechanisms at cryogenic temperatures.
Compared with a rapidly quenched baseline, SRO-engineered samples will retain a single-phase microstructure more effectively during long-term high-temperature aging.
Compared with a rapidly quenched baseline, SRO-engineered samples will accumulate fewer irradiation-induced defects and show higher high-temperature strength and better cryogenic toughness.
